title: Internal-State Probes Read the Situation, Not the Action
hook: Probes that seem to detect an LLM's harmful intent before it acts mostly just detect the prompt's topic — three careful tests find they don't predict future misbehavior.
key_points: Tested three probing methods across three model families, including fine-tune/base direction probes and steering vectors.
One probe separates fine-tune from base at AUC 1.000 — but fires on 0 of 143 real pre-action contexts where the model later misbehaves.
Another decodes prompt domain almost perfectly (AUC 0.999) but its future-behavior signal barely beats guessing the majority class.
Steering effects that look semantically meaningful lose specificity against unrelated concepts like weather or sports.
content_html: Interpretability probes that flag harmful intent inside a model's activations sound like an ideal safety net — catch the bad action before it's generated. This paper tests that promise rigorously, and finds it doesn't hold up.
extra_html: The authors test three probing methods across three model families: a fine-tune-versus-base direction on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, last-token probes on unsafe prefills for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-27B-IT emotion-concept vectors used for projection and steering in a blackmail scenario. Each looks impressive on its own construction test — the Qwen direction hits AUC 1.000 separating fine-tune from base — but none survive stronger checks for genuine pre-action prediction. That same Qwen probe crosses its threshold on 0 of 143 audited pre-assistant-turn contexts and 0 of 342 prefill rows where the model actually continues an unsafe trajectory. The Llama probe decodes prompt domain almost perfectly (AUC 0.999) but its best future-behavior version reaches only AUC 0.801 with a mere 5.1-point lift over the majority baseline, and barely transfers across domains. The Gemma emotion projections look semantically coherent but can't distinguish a shared-prefix minimal pair before the differing input arrives, and their steering specificity weakens against unrelated concepts like cats, weather, or sports. The paper's contribution is a methodology for converting "my probe detects X" claims into pre-action tests — and a clear warning that construction validity alone isn't evidence a safety monitor works. Max Fomin, Elad David, and Amit LeVi, arXiv 2026.

related.title: SAE Interventions Are Unreliable
related.hook: Clamping a 'harmful' sparse-autoencoder feature looks like it stops bad behavior — but this paper recovers it 95.8% of the time, exposing the gap between feature-level and real control.

related.title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
related.hook: Finding the prompts that make a model misbehave is slow if humans do it by hand. So use another language model to generate those attacks automatically — at scale.

related.title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Features from Claude 3 Sonnet
related.hook: Does dictionary learning survive at production scale? Anthropic found millions of features in Claude 3 Sonnet — and could steer the model by turning one up.

flashcards.prompt: What distinction does this paper test — 'reading the prompt' versus what?
flashcards.back_html: Whether a probe genuinely predicts a model's future harmful action before it happens, versus merely detecting the topic or setup of the current prompt.

flashcards.prompt: Why is a probe with AUC 1.000 on one test still reported as a negative result here?

choices.text: It separates fine-tune from base perfectly but fails to fire on real pre-action contexts where the model actually misbehaves later
Because AUC 1.000 is mathematically impossible and signals a bug
Because the authors don't trust AUC as a metric at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Construction-validity AUC doesn't guarantee the probe generalizes to real pre-action monitoring — it can look perfect on its training setup and still miss actual unsafe trajectories.

flashcards.prompt: Why does this matter for AI safety monitoring in practice?
flashcards.back_html: A monitor that looks strong on construction-validity tests can still fail to catch real misalignment before it happens — teams need generalization and specificity checks, not just a high AUC.
